turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Love that you’re jumping into this! Let’s keep it really simple.

Here are the main choices you’ll see and what they mean:

By growth habit (shape of the plant)
Shrub roses: Bushy plants, usually 3–5 feet tall. Great for most gardens, easy to care for, lots of blooms.
Climbing roses: Long canes that need support like an arch, fence, or trellis. Perfect if you want a rose-covered arch or wall.
Groundcover / landscape roses: Low, spreading plants. Good for covering a slope or the front of a border.
Hybrid tea roses: The classic “long-stem” rose look, usually one big bloom per stem. Great if you want cut flowers for vases.
By bloom style
Single or simple blooms: Fewer petals, open centers, very natural look and loved by pollinators.
Full, many-petaled blooms: Big, “old-fashioned” or English-style flowers that look very lush.
By blooming habit
Continuous bloomers: Keep blooming all season without long breaks.
Repeat bloomers: Bloom in waves (a big flush of flowers, then a rest, then more flowers).
By fragrance
Some roses are lightly scented, some are very strong and perfumey.
On our site you can filter by fragrance level if scent is important to you.
By color
You can choose anything from soft pastels (pinks, creams, apricots) to bold colors (red, yellow, orange, purple).
By size
We list sizes in feet. This tells you how tall and wide the plant will be when mature so you know if it fits your space.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question. Let’s keep your very first time super simple.

I’ll assume you have:

One rose from us (in a 1‑gallon container)
Optional: the Get Growing Bundle

If you’re planting in the ground

Pick the spot
At least 6 hours of sun.
Soil that does not stay soggy after rain.
Check timing
Plant in the ground only after your last spring frost or at least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.
If you’re outside that window, keep the rose in a larger pot outdoors for now (see container steps below).
Prepare the hole
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep.
Mix the top soil from the hole with:
About 1 cup of Bone Meal (from the bundle)
Some cow manure and/or mint compost from the bundle to enrich the soil.
Plant the rose
Take the rose out of its shipping container or compostable bag.
Set it in the hole so the existing soil line on the rose is at ground level (not buried deeper).
Backfill with your amended soil and press gently to remove air pockets.
Water and feed
Water slowly and deeply around the base until the soil is evenly moist.
Mix Founders Fish Fertilizer from the bundle at 4 oz per gallon of water and use this as your watering once at planting.
Mulch
Use Mint Compost as a 1–2 inch layer on top of the soil around the plant, keeping it a couple of inches away from the main stems.

If you’re planting in a container (for a patio, or temporary holding)

Choose the pot
At least 10–15 gallons for a bush rose.
Must have drainage holes.
Fill with soil
Use a good organic potting soil with no granular or time‑release fertilizer.
Mix in some cow manure and 1 cup of Bone Meal into the soil.
Plant
Remove the rose from its shipping container.
Set it so the existing soil line is at the new soil surface.
Backfill and press gently.
Water and feed
Water well after planting.
Use Founders Fish Fertilizer at 4 oz per gallon of water at planting, then every 3–4 weeks in the growing season.
Top dress
Use Mint Compost on the surface of the potting soil as a thin layer; refresh every few months.

For the first few weeks

Keep soil evenly moist but not constantly soaked.
Always water at the base, not over the leaves.
Keep the rose outdoors only; roses need outdoor conditions and dormancy to stay healthy.
